## <a id="_Toc225344730"></a>Executive Summary

The National Institutes of Health \(NIH\) is the largest public funder of biomedical research in the world\. Its mission is to seek fundamental knowledge about the nature and behavior of living systems and apply that knowledge to enhance health, lengthen life, and reduce illness and disability\. Research Enhancement Awards \(R15\) are designed to support meritorious research while concurrently strengthening the research environment of educational institutions and exposing students to research\.

## <a id="_Toc225344731"></a>Background

NIH is an agency within the U\.S\. Department of Health and Human Services\. Often summarized by its tagline, "Turning Discovery Into Health," the agency focuses on research that spans from basic mechanistic studies to clinical applications\. NIH is centrally located in Bethesda, Maryland, where it operates an intramural research program in its own laboratories, accounting for about 10% of its budget\. However, the vast majority of its funding, approximately 80\-85%, is dedicated to extramural research conducted by scientists at educational institutions, hospitals, and other research organizations across the nation and the world to further institutional capacity building\.

## <a id="_Toc225344732"></a>Organization and Structure

NIH is composed of __27 distinct Institutes and Centers \(ICs\)__ and the __Office of the Director \(OD\)__\. Each IC has its own:

- __Specific Mission:__ Focusing on particular disease areas \(e\.g\., National Cancer Institute\), organ systems \(e\.g\., National Eye Institute\), or stages of life \(e\.g\., National Institute on Aging\)\.
- __Independent Budget:__ Receiving separate appropriations from Congress\.
- __Funding Strategy:__ Maintaining its own research priorities and making autonomous funding decisions based on peer review results and public health needs\.

Of these 27 components, __24 have the authority to award extramural grants__\. For a grant to be funded, the project must align with the mission of at least one IC that participates in the R15 program\.

The Extramural Team: PIs will primarily interact with three key roles: 

- Program Official \(PO\): Responsible for the programmatic and scientific aspects of a grant; they recommend applications for funding based on mission fit and are typically the preferred first point of contact for applicants\. Applicants are encouraged to reach out early \(often with a Specific Aim draft\) to confirm alignment with the program’s mission\.
- Scientific Review Officer \(SRO\): Manages the peer review process, ensuring technical merit is evaluated without conflict of interest\.
- Grants Management Officer \(GMO\): Handles the business and administrative compliance aspects of the award\.

## <a id="_Toc225344733"></a>The R15 Programs

The R15 mechanism supports small\-scale research projects at institutions that have not been major recipients of NIH support\. It is divided into two distinct programs:

1. __Academic Research Enhancement Award \(AREA\):__ Specifically for undergraduate\-focused institutions \(non\-health professional or graduate schools\) where undergraduate students comprise the majority of the research team\.
2. __Research Enhancement Award Program \(REAP\):__ For health professional and graduate schools; students must be involved, but there is no requirement that participants be primarily undergraduates\.

__Note: UNT only applies to the AREA R15s__

### <a id="_Toc225344734"></a>Objectives of the AREA R15

- Provide support for meritorious research at undergraduate\-focused institutions or institutional components
- Strengthen the research environment at these institutions/components
- Give undergraduate students an opportunity to gain significant biomedical research experience through active involvement in the research

__ __

- If your project does NOT include a clinical trial, apply using https://grants\.nih\.gov/grants/guide/pa\-files/PAR\-25\-134\.html

## <a id="_Toc225344738"></a>Award Size

- Funding Level: Up to $375,000 direct costs, excluding consortium Facilities and Administrative \(F&A\) costs, for the entire project period of up to 3 years\. 
- Project Period: Limited to 3 years\.
- NIH’s Modular Budget Policy: 
	- If requesting <=$250,000 direct costs minus consortium F&A: Use the modular budget format\.
	- If requesting >$250,000\-$375,000 direct costs minus consortium F&A: Use the R&R \(detailed\) budget format\.,
- __Special Notice:__ The total budget for all years of the project must be requested in Budget Period 1\.  \(This is different from most NIH grant application budgets\.\)

[https://grants\.nih\.gov/funding/activity\-codes/R15\#:~:text=Award%20Information,Other%20Resources%20\(DOCX%2C%2044KB\)](https://grants.nih.gov/funding/activity-codes/R15#:~:text=Award%20Information,Other%20Resources%20(DOCX%2C%2044KB))

## <a id="_Toc225344739"></a>Eligibility

__Institutional Eligibility:__ The applicant organization must have received no more than $6 million in annual NIH funding in 4 of the past 7 fiscal years\. GCA will confirm eligibility\. [https://grants\.nih\.gov/grants/funding/Determing\-Organization\-Funding\-Levels\-R15\-Eligibility\.pdf](https://grants.nih.gov/grants/funding/Determing-Organization-Funding-Levels-R15-Eligibility.pdf)

__![](data:image/png;base64,)PI Eligibility:__ The PI must have a primary appointment at an R15\-eligible institution and cannot be the PI of any other active NIH research grant at the time of the award\. The PI may, however, serve as Key Personnel on other NIH grants\.

[https://grants\.nih\.gov/grants/funding/R15\-Eligibility\-Decision\-Tree\.pdf](https://grants.nih.gov/grants/funding/R15-Eligibility-Decision-Tree.pdf)

Key Considerations: 

- Be sure to use the appropriate NOFO \(notice of funding opportunity\) for your college and for your project type \(clinical trial or not\)\.
- Review and confirm principal investigator eligibility requirements\.
- Complete your [GSC request](https://forms.cloud.microsoft/Pages/ResponsePage.aspx?id=khnecMYHD0ijGKGvy6A5g4I5-kEkSrREsf7_HPnnlWVUN1dOSllVSEpYMjZNNlRMVkZEMFFST0ZLNSQlQCN0PWcu) as soon as you plan to submit\. Your assigned pre\-award specialist will assist and upload the required institutional eligibility letter when assembling the application package\.

## <a id="_Toc225344740"></a>How Proposals are Reviewed

As of January 25, 2025, NIH utilizes the Simplified Review Framework for R15 applications to reduce reputational bias and focus on scientific merit\.

###  <a id="_Toc225344741"></a>Scoring Criteria \(1\-9 Scale\)

Factor Strength/Overall Impact

High

Medium

Low

Score

1 2 3

4 5 6

7 8 9

- __Factor 1: Importance of the Research \(Scored\): __Reviewers ask “Should it be done?” evaluating Significance and Innovation\.
- __Factor 2: Rigor and Feasibility \(Scored\):__ Reviewers ask “Can it be done well?” evaluating the Approach, including rigor of prior research and reproducibility\.
- __Factor 3: Expertise and Resources \(Not Numerically Scored\):__ Reviewers evaluate the Investigators and Environment as "appropriate" or "not appropriate"\. In making this determination, reviewers ask “Does the team have the expertise and institutional resources needed to successfully complete the project?” Although this factor is not numerically scored, a rating of “not appropriate” may reduce favor with reviewer and could negatively influence the overall impact score\.

### <a id="_Toc225344742"></a>The Two\-Level Review Process

1. First Level: A Scientific Review Group \(SRG\) or "study section" of expert peers evaluates scientific merit and assigns an impact score\.
2. Second Level: An Advisory Council of the specific IC reviews the application for relevance to the Institute's mission and national priorities before the IC Director makes the final funding decision\.

[https://grants\.nih\.gov/grants\-process/review](https://grants.nih.gov/grants-process/review)

## <a id="_Toc225344743"></a>Strong Training Component for R15

Student engagement is the key\. The research team must be composed primarily of __undergraduate students from the applicant institution\.__ Considering the following questions: 

- How will you recruit a diverse group of students?
- From which different levels of study will you recruit?
- What roles will the students play in the research project? \(Research design, collecting data, presenting, participating in lab meetings?\)
- What kind of training do students need to successfully support the project? \(e\.g\. CITI training\)

<a id="_Toc225344744"></a>Detailed Student Engagement Checklists:

- Student involvement in research may include participation in the design of experiments and controls, collection and analysis of data, execution and troubleshooting of experiments, presenting at meetings, drafting journal articles, participation in lab meetings to discuss results and future experiments, etc\. Reviewers expect clear and specific evidence that students will play meaningful roles rather than serving in limited or purely technical capacities\.
- The AREA program is a research grant program, not a training or fellowship program, and, as such, applications should not include training plans such as didactic training or non\-research activities relating to professional development\.
- The proposed research should be appropriate for a research team comprised primarily of undergraduate students\.  
- Reviewers will assess the likely availability of undergraduates to participate in the research project and evaluate plans for informing undergraduate students of opportunities to participate in the research project\.
- In the Research Strategy: 
	- Describe how the proposed plan can achieve the specific aims yielding rigorous data that can be disseminated, with a research team composed primarily of undergraduate students within the timeframes proposed\. 
	- Describe how undergraduate students will be supervised while conducting research\. 
	- Describe how undergraduate students will participate in research activities such as planning, execution, and/or analysis of the research\. 
	- Formal training plans \(e\.g\., non\-research activities, didactic training, seminars\) should not be provided, although a brief description of activities related to enhancing students' research capabilities and progress \(e\.g\., the use of individual development plans, etc\.\) is permitted\. 
	- Describe plans to ensure a safe laboratory environment and that all research personnel follow laboratory safety best\-practices\. 
- In the Personnel Justification \(Modular\) or Budget Justification \(R&R Non\-modular budget\):
	- Indicate aspects of the proposed research in which undergraduate students will participate\. 
	- If participating students have not yet been individually identified, the number and academic level of those to be involved should be provided\.
- In the Personal Statement of the Biosketch:
	- Each PD/PI should include a summary of their experience supervising and engaging undergraduate students in research in the Personal Statement\. 
	- The PD\(s\)/PI\(s\) should indicate how undergraduate student researchers helped disseminate research results\. Products for dissemination may include, among others, presentations, posters, publications, and datasets\.

## <a id="_Toc225344745"></a>Common Proposal Pitfalls

- __Not Contacting the Program Officer \(PO\):__ Failing to contact the PO early in the proposal development process is a common mistake\. Early communication can help ensure program fit, clarify expectations, and identify potential concerns before submission\.
- __Insufficient Justification for Project Duration:__ Multi\-year funding requests must be clearly justified\. Reviewers may be critical if the scope of work does not convincingly support the requested project period or if the timeline lacks detail and feasibility\.
- __Vague Student Integration:__ For R15s, a weak plan for student involvement is a major red flag\. Reviewers look for specific roles students will play in data collection, lab meetings, and their path toward co\-authorship\. A frequently noted issue by NIH is that some projects are too complex or specialized to be carried out by undergraduate or graduate students\.
- __Dependent Aims:__ A common technical error is designing a project where the success of Specific Aim 2 depends entirely on a positive outcome from Specific Aim 1\. If the first aim fails or yields unexpected results, the entire proposal becomes unworkable in the eyes of the reviewer\.
- __Descriptive vs\. Hypothesis\-Driven:__ Reviewers often penalize "fishing expeditions"—aims that are merely descriptive or seeking to collect data without a clear, testable hypothesis or measurable outcome\.
- __Over\-Focus on Disease:__ A frequent mistake is writing the Project Abstract or Significance section focused entirely on the clinical disease rather than the specific scientific problem or gap in knowledge being addressed\.
- __Neglecting Compensation:__ Failing to provide a clear, fair plan for student compensation \(e\.g\., at least minimum wage or justified course credit\) can undermine the feasibility of the training component\.
- __Overreliance on outside collaborators: __Heavy dependence on external partners can weaken the application, especially since a key goal of the program is to strengthen the research environment at the applicant’s institution\.

## <a id="_Toc225344746"></a>Tips for Successful Proposal Development

- __Master the Specific Aims:__ Treat this as your "elevator pitch"\. Use a clear rhetorical pattern: orient the reader with a brief background, identify the "hook" \(the gap in knowledge\), present a well\-founded central hypothesis, and outline complementary but independent aims\.
- __Address Rigor Explicitly:__ Within the Research Strategy, you must move beyond a simple rationale\. Explicitly discuss the rigor of prior research \(scientific premise\) and the rigor of the proposed research, including sample sizes, power calculations, control groups, and measures to control bias\.
- __Include Preliminary Data:__ Although preliminary data are not required for R15 applications, they are often included to demonstrate feasibility\. They may be presented in the Significance or Approach sections, as appropriate\. Expectations vary by NIH Institute and Center; some prefer preliminary data, while others support early\-stage projects without it\. Applicants should consult with the Program Officer \(PO\) to determine expectations\.
- __Tailor Your Biosketch:__ Do not use a generic version\. The Personal Statement should specifically describe why you are well\-suited for this project and highlight your experience mentoring undergraduate or graduate students\.
- __Optimize Your Figures:__ Use figures strategically to provide a "snapshot" of the full study at the beginning of the Approach section\. Ensure all captions are readable and that figures directly support concepts that are complex to explain in text\.
- __Emphasize the Institutional Environment:__ In the Facilities & Other Resources section, explicitly describe how the award will strengthen the research environment and provide unique opportunities for a diverse group of students to gain biomedical experience\. Be sure to follow the instructions in the NOFO\. These deviate from the SF\-424 Application Guide\. Use subheadings to address each bullet point\.

## <a id="_Toc225344747"></a>Tips for Engagement

Engaging with NIH staff is a critical, yet often underutilized, step for PIs\.

- Use NIH Matchmaker: This tool in the RePORTER database allows PIs to enter an abstract or specific aims to find ICs, study sections, and Program Officials whose portfolios align with their topic\. [https://grants\.nih\.gov/news\-events/nih\-extramural\-nexus\-news/2026/02/make\-a\-perfect\-pair\-with\-nih\-matchmaker](https://grants.nih.gov/news-events/nih-extramural-nexus-news/2026/02/make-a-perfect-pair-with-nih-matchmaker)
- Contact the PO Early: PIs should send a "concept paper" or draft Specific Aims page to a PO at least six weeks before the submission deadline\. Ask about mission fit, the appropriate funding mechanism, and responsiveness to review criteria\.
- Address Student Involvement: For R15s, reviewers look for clear plans on how students will be recruited and involved in the research, including their roles in data collection and co\-authorship on publications\.

## <a id="_Toc225344748"></a>Key Application Components

### <a id="_Toc225344749"></a>Eligibility and Institutional Verification

- __PI Appointment:__ The Principal Investigator must have a primary appointment at an R15\-eligible institution\.
- __IHE Eligibility Letter:__ A formal Letter of Support verifying the institution's R15 eligibility is a required component of the application\.

### <a id="_Toc225344750"></a>Key Personnel

- __Personal Statement:__ Unlike a standard R01, the PI and all senior/key personnel must include a summary of their previous and/or current experience supervising undergraduate and/or graduate students in research within their Personal Statement\.
- __Use SciENcv:__ Applicants are required to use SciENcv to generate these digitally certified, 5\-page Biographical Sketches\.

[https://grants\.nih\.gov/grants/how\-to\-apply\-application\-guide/forms\-i/research\-forms\-i\.pdf](https://grants.nih.gov/grants/how-to-apply-application-guide/forms-i/research-forms-i.pdf)

### <a id="_Toc225344751"></a>Page Limit

- Project Summary/Abstract: 30 lines of text
- Project Narrative: three sentences
- Introduction to Resubmission and Revision Applications: 1 page
- Specific Aims: 1 page
- Research Strategy: 12 pages
- Biographical Sketch Common Form & Biographical Sketch Supplement: No hard limit; Biosketch page length is controlled through SciENcv\.

Be sure to read and follow the latest instructions for the Biosketch Common Form and Biosketch Supplement\.

[https://grants\.nih\.gov/grants\-process/write\-application/how\-to\-apply\-application\-guide/page\-limits](https://grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/how-to-apply-application-guide/page-limits)

### <a id="_Toc225344752"></a>Appendix Policy

The NIH has a highly restrictive appendix policy\. Only the following are allowable: 

- Blank data collection forms, surveys, or questionnaires
- Blank informed consent or assent forms
- Clinical trial protocols or investigator brochures
- Warning: Including disallowed materials in the appendix will result in your application being withdrawn without review

## <a id="_Toc225344753"></a>Early Career and Special Programs \(including but not limited to R15\)

- Early Stage Investigator \(ESI\) Status: NIH is committed to supporting ESIs—PIs within 10 years of their terminal degree who have not yet held a substantial NIH independent research award\. ESIs may receive prioritized funding and special consideration during review\. [https://grants\.nih\.gov/policy\-and\-compliance/policy\-topics/early\-stage\-investigators](https://grants.nih.gov/policy-and-compliance/policy-topics/early-stage-investigators)
- __R01__\-Stephen I\. Katz ESI Research Project Grant: A program specifically for ESIs proposing a project in a new direction for which they have no preliminary data\. [https://grants\.nih\.gov/funding/activity\-codes/R01/katz\-esi\-r01](https://grants.nih.gov/funding/activity-codes/R01/katz-esi-r01)
- Targeted Notices: ICs often issue Notices of Special Interest \(NOSIs\) to highlight specific scientific areas they want to prioritize, such as NIGMS’s support for AREA data science research proposals\.
